en: The Litany of Heramba.
First Section (in the Śaśivadanā meter):
May the Lord of the Gaṇas, who possesses an auspicious name and a supreme abode, bestow upon me incomparable glory. || 1 ||
May the elephant-faced one grant me the yoga that has conquered the affliction of old age and destroyed disease. || 2 ||
May Gaṇapati grant me devotion to his own feet, as well as preeminent power of the arms. || 3 ||
May the all-pervading son of Hari bestow upon me that most heart-pleasing, supremely pure knowledge of reality. || 4 ||
May my lord, whose face is that of an elephant, grant me the faultless science of predicting future constellations. || 5 ||
O son of Hara, you who are like the moon that dispels the frost of sin for those who have conquered their own senses, make this [world] invincible!
O elephant-faced one, make this poet your servant—he who has acquired the state of lips that are exceedingly sweet with honey. 7.
I contemplate the form of Gaṇapati in my mind; I spread the fame of Gaṇapati with my speech. || 8 ||
May my Gaṇanātha pacify my sin; may he also instantly neutralize the curses of others. 9.
May this new composition, whose face is like the moon, worship Gaṇeśa as a woman worships her husband. 10.

The second section (in the Madalekhā meter): The wise person says of you— that you are asleep in the abode of the Mūlādhāra when the elephant of the intellect is sluggish, yet shining forth when it is engaged in discernment.
There is a Guru in the sky, and you alone are he here on earth;
appearing as a transformation of Gaṇeśa, you shine forth among those who are true devotees.
A certain powerful one, dwelling in the *mūlādhāra*, shines as the remover of sins, embraced by the brides of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāsiddhi*). 13.
O Son of the Lord, my hope is to behold your boundless power within your body, and to drink the stream of nectar from the crown of your head. 14.
She who is your mother is Cit; he who is the most excellent is your father, Siddhi; Bāhyamati is she who is your sister, O Lord; and Pramadā is she who is your wife. (15)
Whether you fulfill that desire in my heart or not,
let this service of mine be accepted by you, O Mattebhānana.
O God, if you do not go to the sky, then why do you perform a dance upon the lap of Skanda’s elder brother? 17.
I have no effort for my own sake; this exertion of mine is for one who has no self-interest.
O son of Śiva, grant me assistance immediately! 18.
Indeed, what man is capable of describing your greatness?
O Elephant-faced One, the fortune of all is in your hands. 19.
May the poet-bees enjoy these intoxicating,
honey-like lines of Madalekhā, just as they enjoy the lunar rays.
The Third Section (in Indravajrā meter):
I bow to the eldest of Rudra’s eleven sons, the lord of mantras, by whose stakes all the scriptures dispel the darkness that obscures the sun. 21.
O Heramba, whatever verse was composed by the wise with his intellect, your contribution therein is shared; and wherever a mantra was made by a seer, your manifestation there is distinguished.

O Lord, son of Rudra, they say that you are "impure" (ucchiṣṭa) by way of a pun when you plunge into the surface of the tongue; but if you are impure, what difference is there between spitting out the Vedic study and being impure? 23.
O Lord, they know this rat, who dwells in a hole and is accompanied by a companion, as the one called Rasana, who devours all grains with his sharp teeth; we recognize him as your vehicle.
O Gaṇeśa, while you dwell in the Ādhāra-cakra as the ever-blazing, luminous soul, your heat alone digests all food; these words of mine are merely intended to praise it. 25.
O son of Śiva, Vaiśvānara is the fire that is the life-force of all, while you are the fire of the organ of speech;
he who knows no difference between the two of you does not become deluded regarding embodied beings in this world.
Some call you the son of the all-pervading Lord under the name Brahmaṇaspati;
others have been told by the wise that you are the minister of the all-pervading Indra under the name Bṛhaspati.
Your tongue alone is the altar purified by water; the company of people there is the smoke;
the pure stories of the Lord of the World are the flame; and where the virtuous offer their hearts as clarified butter. (28)

That very form of Indra consisting of lightning, which was described by the silent ones (the Munis), is your own true nature. The distinction between you and Indra that has been asserted is rooted in the difference between the body of lightning and the vital breath.

May these Indravajrā meters, possessing the luster of divine fire, worship Karīndrānana—the son of Bharga whose wife is Dhiṣaṇā and whose body is like the foremost of divine fires, and who is the friend of those who bow before him. 30.
The Fourth Section (in the Vasantatilaka meter):
O Lord, why do you roar with agitation when your own manifestation has been shattered and submerged in great calamity?
O Giver of Boons, if I fall asleep, wake me with a slap on the hand; if I go onto the wrong path, turn me back quickly.
O Lord, if this is another costume, let the dance begin; why do you maintain such silence appropriate for it?
O Master, let these attendants draw aside the curtain;
why is delay being made when You are present in person? 32.
This darkness, which robs the power of vision, blocks the path within my heart; I am unable to see.
O Lord, there is some state of affection; grant me a fragment of the light of Your compassionate glance, so that I may proceed before You.
If I do not perform severe austerity, it would be an offense against you; O son of Rudra, why did you not urge me?
And if, having been urged by you, I were not to act accordingly—
O elephant-faced one, what power do you have to incite others? || 34 ||
I have no task whatsoever; indeed, I possess no form of the gods, nor do I have any dress of yours.
O elephant-faced one, for whom, then, is this desired, or rather, is it a hardship?
But something remains of mine that still clings to the human body. (35)
Or rather, what is the use of even the mention of that elephant-faced one for you, while this most perishable bodice remains?
If your fame is to become as white as the moon, like that of Viṣṇu.
Let it go to dissolution within the very luster of your teeth. || 36 ||

O Lord, O enemy of the wicked, having seized the gross body— the abode of all the desires of the vital breaths— as well as the mind, the intellect, joy, and their very root, and having taken possession of the entire treasury;
O King of Obstacles, display your majesty before me.
The goddess Mati has eyes as broad as a lotus leaf on water,
and the goddess Siddhi has a face like the stainless moon;
these two attend the blazing Lord of Day (the Sun), just as heat and cold attend him.
O Lord with the face of a lion, I constantly worship you. || 38 ||
While Rudra, who bears the guise of a lord of Siddhas and is beloved by the earth,
was presiding over Mount Kailāsa, Vajrapāṇi’s son, assuming the form of a lordly elephant-faced one, [attacked him].
Having become all-pervading, he leads all his attendants without exception.
May these *vasantatilakā* verses, composed by the elephant among poets, gladden the heart of the god Gajavaktra (Gaṇeśa) and the heart of the lord of the heart who possesses the intellect of success.
The songs were sung by someone endowed with pure contemplation.
Thus ends "The Worship of Heramba," the work of Gaṇapati, disciple of the venerable great seer Ramaṇa, belonging to the lineage of Vasiṣṭha, and son of Narasiṃha.
